_purpose: Per Phase 2-E Codex 2nd review: each synthetic-secret fixture is
tracked here with a SHA-256 hash and a stable invalidity justification.
bench/run.py refuses to execute unless every listed file's hash matches.
This prevents a malicious or careless edit from turning a synthetic
fixture into a real, leakable credential.

fixtures.invalidity_reason: Body 'BENCHMARKSECSCAN' is a literal English string AWS would never issue; the secret-key half is similarly obvious. Phase 2-F rotated away from the official AWS doc example because gitleaks (correctly) allowlists those.
Body 'secscanbenchmarkfixture' is a deterministic English string, not the random hex GitHub issues. Phase 2-F rotated away from the all-zero body to avoid the gitleaks docs allowlist.
Body 'SECSCANbenchmarkfixture' is a deterministic English string, not the issued hex pattern.

fixtures.source: Synthetic — body = first 36 hex chars of sha256('secscan-bench')
fixtures.invalidity_reason: Body is a deterministic hex string derived from a public marker; it is structurally valid for the gitleaks npm-access-token rule (passes the entropy threshold) but is NOT a real npm token. Two earlier phases of this fixture (all-zero body, then 'secscanbenchmark' body) failed to trigger gitleaks because the all-zero body is allowlisted and the English-string body falls below the entropy threshold.
